feedback: For a wrong match between 5(n+4) and 5n+4, substitute n=5 and compare 45 with 29 to show which reading needs brackets.
If a learner chooses 10 for a² at a=5, remind that a² = a×a = 25, whereas 2a = a+a = 10.
If a learner chooses 3+y for 3y, unfold 3y into y+y+y and test with a value (at y=4, 3y=12 but 3+y=7).
activities.intendedInsight: Matching words, symbols and an area/array model makes the coefficient/power/grouping conventions explicit, with left-to-right and symbol-misreading answers as sharp contrasts to the correct reading.
learnerActions: Match word descriptions to their expressions, e.g. connect 'four more than the number, all multiplied by five' to 5(n+4) and 'five times the number, then add four' to 5n+4, plus n² and 3n.
Match the same expression across representations — a word description, its symbolic form, and an area/array model — so each expression is met in more than one representation (following Swan/MAP).
Answer: what does 3y mean? (Correct: y+y+y; distractors: 3+y, and '3y read as a two-digit number'.)
Answer: what is the value of a² when a=5? (Correct: 25; distractor: 10, which is 2a.)
Translate 'the number divided by 5, then add 4' and 'add 4 to the number, then divide the whole thing by 5' into symbols and explain how the notation shows the difference.
activities.title: Word↔symbol↔area-model matching and targeted multiple choice

feedback: When a learner says '3 plus y' for 3y, substitute y=4 and ask whether 3y is 12 or 7, then restate '3y is three lots of y'.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the notation precisely rehearses meaning rather than guessing, and a substitution challenge exposes a slip immediately.
learnerActions: Read expressions aloud precisely, e.g. say '3y' as 'three lots of y' and 'y²' as 'y times itself'.
Respond when challenged on a misreading: 'you said 3 plus y — if y is 4, is 3y twelve or seven?' and resolve it by substituting.
Translate both ways in speech: symbols→words and words→symbols.
activities.title: Read it aloud: oral rehearsal of precise reading

feedback: If a learner talks about n as 'the letter' or a label and is unsure it can be added or multiplied, reassert that n is a hidden number and substitute a value to show the operation working. A review of using letters for unknowns from earlier work may help.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a letter stands for a number, expressions can be operated on and evaluated like arithmetic; treating the letter as an object/label ('a' = apple) blocks this.
learnerActions: State that each letter is a hidden NUMBER, then substitute a chosen value to make operations on it concrete.
Rewrite an answer that keeps the letter as a tag/label into one that treats the letter as a number that can be added and multiplied.
Check a reading by substituting a value and asking whether the reading makes sense.
activities.title: The letter is a hidden number
